result:
`final.py` scores **0.5856 on the search split, against 0.365 for the LRU baseline. I used 10 of the 24 scorer calls.** I stopped with 14 unused because my last several variants all scored within about 0.001 of each other on my own test traces. More calls at that point would only have fitted the search split. I haven't checked the unseen instances, so that score is still unknown.

| | Search score | My held-out test traces |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 | – |
| First strong single policy (W-TinyLFU with a self-tuning window) | 0.5285 | – |
| Best single policy (LIRS) | 0.5655 | 0.551 |
| **Final (combines several policies)** | **0.5856** | **0.570** |

**How the final cache works.** It runs five policies side by side in the background: LIRS, LIRS with a very small new-key area, W-TinyLFU with a self-tuning window, a frequency-heavy TinyLFU, and ARC. Each one keeps its own hit rate, weighted toward recent requests. The real cache only adds a key if the current best policy would hold it. When that policy drops a key, the key stays in the real cache as filler until the space is needed. To keep it from switching back and forth, it only changes leader when another policy is clearly ahead.

This stays within the rules: only the requested key is ever added, the cache never goes over capacity, and I checked hits and size on every request. No single policy wins every pattern. Recency-heavy traffic suits LRU/ARC, loops mixed with hot keys suit the frequency-based policy, and shifting loops suit LIRS. On every trace type my combined cache came within about 0.01 of the best policy for that type. It runs about 600,000 requests in roughly 2.2 seconds locally, well under the 8-second limit.

**Different approaches I tried:**

| Approach | Search score |
|---|---|
| ARC | 0.407 |
| S3-FIFO | 0.441 |
| W-TinyLFU, fixed window | 0.503 |
| W-TinyLFU, self-tuning window | 0.5285 |
| LIRS | 0.5655 |

These three were tested only on my own traces and dropped:
- LIRS with a self-tuning new-key area: about +0.001.
- LIRS with a frequency filter on new keys: worse.
- LFU with dynamic aging: much worse on loops.

**Combined versions, in order:**

| Version | Search score |
|---|---|
| 3 policies | 0.5708 |
| + frequency-heavy TinyLFU | 0.5815 |
| + small-new-key LIRS | 0.5853 |
| + keeping dropped keys as filler | 0.5856 |

Adding S3-FIFO or a plain LFU, swapping ARC for LRU, and retuning how fast it switches leaders made no difference on my traces.

**About the held-out check.** The `score` command only scores the search split, so I couldn't score the unseen instances myself. The held-out column comes from my own test traces, using seeds I never tuned on. It ranked the candidates in the same order as the official scorer.

**Gaps that are left.** Two trace types, "hot_with_scans" (0.25) and "mixed" (0.28), stayed flat across every policy. On my versions of those traces, the theoretical best is far higher than any real policy got.

Everything is in the `cache` folder: `final.py`, my test traces (`harness.py`, `tune.py`, `check.py`), every candidate (`c_*.py`), and the scorer's own record in `calls.log`.
